title: Musical idols and working backward to New Orleans roots
summary: From Harry James to Spanier, Armstrong, Oliver and New Orleans primitives; not fond of Beiderbecke; first New Orleans visit in 1950.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: did you have any idols when you were coming up

oh yeah I um it's funny I sort of worked backwards in my um taste I was first attracted to Harry James he played you know fantastic trumpet player let's face it man played brilliantly and I thought that was really great and then I heard uh those Muggsy Spanier records that I mentioned the ragtimers and I thought wow this is a whole different thing and I liked that and then finally I worked my way back to uh some Louis Armstrong and the Hot Five and Hot Seven things like that really liked those and then started getting back earlier to King Oliver and then I started hearing some of what I'd have to call the New Orleans primitives some of the people who never left the city and played how one might imagine a neighborhood band might have played in 1910 and I learned to really appreciate that kind of thing and as I got farther and farther back into the roots then I found it easier for me to understand the music and then begin to construct my own style on top of that and I always used to be annoyed when little little phrases or things from say Harry James or Muxi Spanier might pop into my playing you know it's pretty hard not to pick up other people's cliches I was never I was never very fond of Vicks Beiderbeck I never wanted to play like Vicks Beiderbeck I can listen to him and really enjoy what he's doing but it's kind of like watching Charlie Chaplin movies I watch them without laughing I appreciate what he's doing but he's not my man like W.C. Fields is or the March Brothers are I don't know if that parallel makes any sense but I just he was Beiderbeck was just over there and I appreciated what he was doing but I didn't ever want to play like that I just really was more attracted to what I felt was a simpler more honest approach to swing and jazz music out of whatever the tune might happen to be and I appreciated the lesson of coming to New Orleans and finding out that jazz is how you play something off the current hit parade which in 1950 my first visit happened to be Mona Lisa or Jambalaya tunes like that and I was able to hear the bands and the roadhouses that you took me to hear playing those tunes it was a revelation
